editorial.headline: Coastal Protection Construction: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making and upkeep of coastal defences, with full foreign ownership open nationally and no Bali moratorium block at higher-risk large scale.
editorial.body:
Coastal protection construction is the practical work of defending shorelines against the forces that reshape them. It covers the construction, maintenance and rebuilding of coastal-protection structures: groynes, breakwaters, seawalls, artificial headlands, beach nourishment, artificial reefs and comparable works. The code therefore addresses a specialised civil-construction activity whose purpose is not simply to build beside the sea, but to shape, reinforce or restore the edge between land and water.

Its scope is deliberately broad enough to follow a protection asset through its working life. A project may begin with a new structure, return later for maintenance, or require reconstruction where an existing defence must be renewed. The listed works also show the range of methods involved. Some structures interrupt or redirect coastal movement; others dissipate wave energy, reinforce a shoreline, replenish a beach or create a protective reef-like barrier. What unites them is their role as coastal-protection infrastructure.

Registration is open across every scale stated in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the activity is not framed as an undertaking reserved only for the largest contractors. The scale categories in the record leave room for businesses of different sizes to register the activity, while the work itself remains defined by its coastal-protection purpose and by the types of construction, maintenance and rebuilding it includes.

Nationally, the PMA position is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, the picture remains open for this activity today: it is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium. The record places the relevant large-scale OSS risk at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, whereas the moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide on a permanent basis. That distinction is the essential local reading. A foreign investor considering coastal-protection construction in Bali is not facing a moratorium block under the stated rule; the activity sits outside the blocked Low and Medium-Low risk band because its large-scale risk is classified higher.
